analogy.p: Imagine a crowd packed tightly in a stadium, with the crowd pushing harder lower down because there are more people stacked above. If you hold a large cushion in the crowd, it is squashed harder from underneath than from above, so the net push is upwards and may lift it. Similarly the water pushes harder on the bottom of an object than on its top, giving a net upward push. The analogy breaks down because a real crowd is not a continuous fluid, and the push in a fluid acts at right angles to all surfaces, not just from below.
analogy.t: Water pushing back like a crowd of people

bullets: Upthrust is the upward force exerted on an object by the fluid it is in (partially or fully submerged).
It exists in any fluid, liquid or gas: air provides upthrust on a balloon, water provides upthrust on a boat.
It is a **force**, measured in newtons (N), and drawn as an arrow acting upwards.
It acts on the object as a whole, but is the resultant of many pressure forces on the surfaces.
Every object in a fluid has upthrust; whether it floats or sinks depends on how upthrust compares with weight.
This is a Physics-only topic (Paper 2).
Key link: pressure in a liquid increases with depth (previous spec point).
core.h: Starting point: a submerged object in a fluid
core.p: When an object is placed in a fluid (a liquid or a gas) it is surrounded by fluid that exerts pressure on every part of its surface. The specification says that a partially or totally submerged object experiences a **greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface**. This difference creates a **resultant force upwards**, which is called **upthrust**. Understanding upthrust lets you explain why some objects float, why some sink, and how boats, submarines and balloons work.

bullets: Step 1: pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of the object is at a higher pressure than the top.
Step 2: force = pressure x area, so the upward force on the bottom is greater than the downward force on the top.
Step 3: the horizontal forces on the sides cancel out, so only the vertical difference remains.
Step 4: the resultant upward force is the upthrust.
Mark-scheme phrasing: "the pressure at the bottom of the object is greater than at the top, so there is a resultant upward force".
If an object touches the bottom of the container so that no fluid gets underneath, the upthrust can be reduced or absent (e.g. a suction cup stuck to a tank floor).
If the pressure on the top and bottom were equal there would be no resultant force from the fluid, and so no upthrust.
core.h: Why upthrust happens: the pressure difference
core.p: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the bottom face of a submerged object is deeper than the top face and experiences a **greater pressure**. Pressure on a surface produces a force (F = p A), acting at right angles to the surface. The upward force on the bottom surface is therefore larger than the downward force on the top surface. The side forces cancel because they act equally in opposite directions at the same depths. The result is a net, or **resultant, force upwards**: the upthrust.

bullets: Pressure at the top p1 = h1 ρ g; at the bottom p2 = h2 ρ g.
Pressure difference Δp = (h2 - h1) ρ g, where (h2 - h1) is the height of the block.
Upthrust = Δp x A = height x A x ρ g = V ρ g.
V ρ g is the weight of fluid displaced by the object (Archimedes' principle, extension beyond the specification wording).
A bigger submerged volume gives a bigger upthrust.
A denser fluid gives a bigger upthrust for the same volume (which is why it is easier to float in the Dead Sea or in seawater).
A calculation question on this will usually give you the pressures or depths and ask for the force.
core.h: Calculating upthrust from pressure differences (Higher tier reasoning)
core.p: You can show where the size of the upthrust comes from. For a block with top face area A at depth h1 and bottom face at depth h2, the pressures are p1 = h1 ρ g and p2 = h2 ρ g. The pressure difference is (h2 - h1) ρ g, and since force = pressure x area, **upthrust = (p2 - p1) x A = (h2 - h1) A ρ g = V ρ g**, where V is the volume of the block. This is the weight of fluid that the block pushes out of the way, which is known as Archimedes' principle. It shows that upthrust depends only on the volume submerged, the fluid density and g.

bullets: Pressure difference = height of object x ρ g, which has no term for depth below the surface.
Upthrust on a fully submerged object is constant if the fluid density and volume stay constant.
Upthrust does depend on how much of the object is under water for partially submerged objects: more submerged, more upthrust.
The weight of the object does not depend on depth either, so a fully submerged object is either always sinking, always rising or neutral.
In reality water density rises slightly with depth and the pressure slightly compresses objects, but at GCSE both are ignored.
Common wrong idea: "the deeper you go, the greater the upthrust"; deeper gives greater pressure, not greater upthrust.
core.h: Upthrust does not depend on depth (once fully submerged)
core.p: Once an object is completely under the surface, moving it deeper changes both the top and bottom pressures, but by the same amount. The **difference** in pressure stays the same because the height of the object is unchanged. So the upthrust on a fully submerged object is the same at 1 m or at 100 m. This explains why a submarine at constant volume has the same upthrust at any depth, and why it can hover without being pushed up or down by depth changes alone.

bullets: Floating (at rest): upthrust = weight; resultant force = 0.
If pushed down a little the upthrust increases (more is submerged), so it bobs back up.
The submerged part of a floating object displaces a weight of fluid equal to the weight of the object.
A floating object is only partially submerged unless it has the same density as the fluid (when it hovers).
Free body diagram: weight arrow downwards from the centre of mass, upthrust arrow upwards, equal lengths.
Boats, ducks, ice cubes and logs float because they displace enough fluid.
Mark phrase: "the upthrust is equal to the weight so the forces are balanced".
core.p: An object **floats** when its weight is balanced by the upthrust. If the upthrust equals the weight, the forces are balanced, the resultant force is zero and (by Newton's first law) a stationary object stays at rest. A floating object sinks until it has displaced enough fluid so that the upthrust equals its weight, and then it stays at that level. Partially submerged objects floating at the surface are in equilibrium with upthrust = weight.

bullets: Sinks: weight > upthrust; resultant force downwards.
Rises: upthrust > weight; resultant force upwards.
Resultant force = larger force - smaller force (they act in opposite directions).
Acceleration = resultant force / mass (Newton's second law).
As the object speeds up, drag from the fluid grows until it balances the resultant force: terminal velocity.
A sinking object still experiences upthrust; it just is not enough.
A diagram with unequal arrows is the standard way to show this: longer weight arrow means sinking.
core.h: Sinking and rising: when the forces are not balanced
core.p: If the weight of an object is **greater than the upthrust**, there is a resultant force downwards and the object sinks. If the upthrust is **greater than the weight** the resultant force is upwards and the object rises until it reaches the surface and floats. The resultant force is the difference between the two, and by Newton's second law F = m a it causes acceleration, though drag from the fluid soon limits the speed and a terminal velocity is reached.

bullets: Object density < fluid density: floats.
Object density > fluid density: sinks.
Object density = fluid density: stays suspended anywhere in the fluid.
Density ρ = mass / volume, so use this to compare materials.
Cork (about 240 kg/m3), wood (around 700 kg/m3) and ice (917 kg/m3) float on water (1000 kg/m3).
Steel (several times denser than water) and aluminium (2700 kg/m3) sink as solid blocks.
Explanations must refer to density, not "heaviness" or "mass".
core.h: Floating and sinking in terms of density
core.p: For an object that is fully submerged, its weight is its density times volume times g, and the upthrust is the fluid density times the same volume times g. So the comparison reduces to a comparison of **densities**. If the object is **less dense than the fluid**, upthrust exceeds weight and it floats (rises to the surface). If it is **denser than the fluid**, the weight exceeds upthrust and it sinks. If the densities are equal, the forces balance and the object hovers (neutral buoyancy). This is why it is density, not weight, that decides floating and sinking: a huge log floats and a small pebble sinks.

bullets: Fraction submerged = density of object / density of fluid (for a uniform object floating freely).
Ice: 917 / 1000 = 0.917, so about 92% of an iceberg is below the surface.
A boat floats higher in seawater (about 1030 kg/m3) than in fresh water, since less water needs to be displaced.
The Plimsoll line on ships shows the safe loading level for different water densities.
The same ship loaded with more cargo has more weight, so it sinks lower to displace more water.
A log of density 700 kg/m3 floats with 70% of its volume submerged.
An object of exactly the same density as the fluid is completely submerged but does not sink or rise.
core.h: How much of a floating object is under the surface?
core.p: A floating object sinks until it has displaced fluid equal in weight to its own weight. For a uniform solid, the fraction of the volume submerged equals the ratio of the object's density to the fluid density. Ice has a density of about 917 kg/m3 and water about 1000 kg/m3, so about 92% of an iceberg is under the water (917 / 1000 = 0.917). A denser fluid supports an object with less of it submerged, because less fluid has to be displaced to equal the same weight.

bullets: A ship's average density = total mass / total volume (including the air-filled space).
The bowl shape displaces a large volume of water for a small mass of steel.
Floating needs displaced water weight = ship weight (upthrust = weight).
Overloading or flooding increases the weight, so the ship sinks lower or sinks completely.
Aluminium foil formed into a boat floats for the same reason; crumpled into a ball it sinks.
Lifejackets, rafts and floats work by adding volume with very little mass, reducing average density.
Exam phrase: "the hull contains a large volume of air so the average density is less than that of water".
core.h: Why steel ships float: average density
core.p: A solid block of steel is denser than water and sinks, but a ship made from the same steel floats because its hull encloses a very large volume of air. What matters is the **average density** of the whole ship (steel plus the air inside). Because the hull is a hollow, bowl-like shape, the ship displaces a large volume of water, so the upthrust equals its weight while it is still only partly submerged. If the hull is breached and fills with water, the average density rises above that of water, and the ship sinks.

bullets: Submarine dives: ballast tanks fill with water, weight increases to more than upthrust.
Submarine rises: compressed air pushes water out, weight decreases to less than upthrust.
Hovering (neutral buoyancy): weight = upthrust, so the submarine stays at constant depth.
Hot air balloon: heating the air makes it less dense, so the average density of balloon plus air is below that of the surrounding air.
Helium balloons rise because helium is less dense than air.
Divers wear weight belts to counter the upthrust from their bodies and wetsuit.
Air is a fluid too: upthrust also acts on objects in air, but it is small because air density is small.
core.h: Controlling floating and sinking: submarines, balloons and fish
core.p: Many machines change their average density to control whether they rise or sink. A submarine has **ballast tanks**: flooding them with seawater increases its weight, so it sinks; blowing the water out with compressed air makes it lighter, so it rises. A hot air balloon is filled with hot air that is less dense than the cooler air outside, giving upthrust greater than weight. Bony fish adjust a gas-filled swim bladder to control their depth.

bullets: Upthrust = weight in air - apparent weight in fluid.
The actual weight of the object does not change; only the force the newtonmeter has to supply does.
If the apparent weight is zero, the object is floating or hovering.
Using the volume submerged and fluid density, V ρ g should equal the upthrust, which can be a check on measurements.
Pushing a ball underwater is hard because upthrust is large for the volume displaced.
The reading drops smoothly as more of the object enters the water, then stays constant once fully submerged.
Graph: apparent weight against depth falls then flattens when fully submerged.
core.p: You can measure upthrust with a newtonmeter. When an object hangs in air, the meter reads its weight. When it is lowered into water, the reading falls because the upthrust helps support it. This lower reading is the **apparent weight**, and the difference between the reading in air and in water is the upthrust. The weight itself has not changed.

bullets: Free body diagram: always include both weight (down) and upthrust (up), with arrow lengths showing which is bigger.
Pressure link: upthrust arises because pressure increases with depth.
Density link: floating or sinking is decided by comparing densities.
Newton's first law: floating at rest means balanced forces.
Newton's second law: unbalanced forces cause acceleration upwards or downwards.
Terminal velocity: sinking objects accelerate until drag balances resultant force.
Atmosphere link: balloons and airships experience upthrust in air for the same reason.
core.h: Links to other topics and examination skills
core.p: Upthrust links pressure, density, weight and resultant forces into one topic. It uses p = h ρ g from the previous point, density ρ = m / V from the particle model, weight W = m g from forces, resultant forces and free body diagrams, and Newton's laws. Many exam questions combine two of these ideas, such as using pressure at two depths to find upthrust, or comparing densities to decide whether an object will float and then explaining what happens to its motion.

exam: "Explain what causes upthrust" (2-3 marks): pressure increases with depth (1); bottom surface deeper, so greater pressure/force than top (1); resultant force upwards (1).
"Explain why an object floats" (2-3 marks): upthrust equals weight (1); resultant force zero / balanced forces (1); density less than fluid (1).
"Explain why an object sinks": weight is greater than upthrust (1); resultant force downward (1); density of the object greater than the fluid (1).
Use the words "resultant force", "balanced" and "density" accurately; vague words like "heavy" or "light" will not earn marks.
For calculation questions: write the equation, substitute, and give units; upthrust = pressure difference x area or volume x ρ g.
4-mark ship question: hull encloses air (1); average density less than water (1); displaces large volume of water (1); upthrust equals weight (1).
Free body diagram marks: arrows start from the object, correct directions, lengths match the balance (equal for floating, unequal for sinking), labelled.
Always compare the two forces with numbers when you are given them, e.g. "upthrust 9.8 N is greater than weight 7.35 N so it rises".
6-mark answers: state pressure increases with depth, explain pressure difference, link to upthrust, compare with weight, link to density, give an example.
Graph tip: apparent weight against depth falls and then becomes constant once the object is fully submerged.
Sanity check: the upthrust on a fully submerged 1 m3 object in water is about 9800 N.

mistakes.r: Floating depends on density: whether the object is less or more dense than the fluid.
mistakes.w: Heavy objects sink and light objects float.

mistakes.r: Only when it is floating or hovering; when sinking weight > upthrust, when rising upthrust > weight.
mistakes.w: Upthrust is always equal to the weight of the object.

mistakes.r: For a fully submerged object, the pressure difference between top and bottom is constant, so upthrust is constant.
mistakes.w: The deeper an object is, the greater the upthrust.

mistakes.r: It still has upthrust; it is just smaller than its weight.
mistakes.w: A sinking object has no upthrust.

mistakes.r: Steel is denser than water; the ship floats because its hull contains air so its average density is less than water.
mistakes.w: Ships float because steel is light or buoyant.

mistakes.r: Weight stays the same; the apparent weight is lower because upthrust supports part of it.
mistakes.w: An object's weight gets smaller in water.

mistakes.r: It arises from a pressure difference: greater pressure on the bottom surface than the top gives a resultant upward force.
mistakes.w: Upthrust is caused by the water pushing up only.

mistakes.r: Weight still acts downwards; it is balanced by an equal upthrust.
mistakes.w: Floating objects have no weight acting on them.

summary: The specification asks you to explain that a partially or totally submerged object experiences greater pressure on its bottom surface than its top surface, creating a resultant upward force called upthrust, and to use this to explain floating and sinking in terms of density and the balance of upthrust and weight. It matters because it explains ships, submarines, balloons and swimming, and links pressure, density and resultant forces into frequent explain and calculate questions.

terms.d: A liquid or a gas, a substance that can flow.
Force per unit area acting at right angles to a surface: p = F / A.
The upward resultant force on a partially or totally submerged object, caused by the greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The force of gravity on an object: W = m g.
Mass per unit volume: ρ = m / V (kg/m3).
Staying at the surface of a fluid because upthrust equals weight (for a partly submerged object).
Moving downwards because weight is greater than upthrust.
Placed beneath the surface of a fluid (partially or totally).
The fluid pushed out of the way by an object placed in it.
Total mass divided by total volume of an object, including any hollow or air-filled spaces.
A tank in a submarine that is filled with water or air to change its weight and therefore make it sink or rise.
The reading on a newtonmeter when an object is in a fluid; weight minus upthrust.
The state where the upthrust equals the weight of a fully submerged object, so it hovers.
The state where forces balance so there is no resultant force.
Upthrust on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

worked.q: A cube of side 0.10 m is held fully submerged in water (density 1000 kg/m3, g = 9.8 N/kg). Its top face is 0.20 m below the surface and its bottom face is 0.30 m below the surface. Calculate (a) the pressure on the top face, (b) the pressure on the bottom face, (c) the upthrust. [5 marks]
steps: Bottom: p = 0.30 x 1000 x 9.8 = 2940 Pa (1 mark).
Area of face = 0.10 x 0.10 = 0.010 m2 (1 mark).
Upthrust = pressure difference x area = 980 x 0.010 = 9.8 N (1 mark).

worked.ans: (a) 7.35 N; (b) it rises, resultant 2.45 N upward; (c) 75% submerged
worked.q: The cube above has a mass of 0.75 kg. (a) Calculate its weight. (b) Will it sink or rise when released? (c) What fraction of the cube will be under water when it floats? [5 marks, Higher tier]
steps: Upthrust 9.8 N is greater than weight 7.35 N (1 mark).
Resultant force = 9.8 - 7.35 = 2.45 N upwards, so it rises (1 mark).

worked.ans: Model answer: The steel block has a higher density than water, so its weight is greater than the upthrust and it sinks. The ship is hollow with a lot of air in the hull, so its average density is less than the density of water. It displaces a large volume of water, so the upthrust is equal to its weight, the forces are balanced, and it floats.
worked.q: Explain why a steel ship floats but a steel block of the same mass sinks. [4 marks]
steps: Marker idea 1: the block is denser than water; weight is greater than upthrust.
Marker idea 2: the ship hull encloses a large volume of air.
Marker idea 3: the ship has a much greater volume, so a lower average density, and displaces a large volume of water.
Marker idea 4: upthrust equals weight for the ship, so it floats.
